# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
# Review: "Two Years On" (Varden 24-Month Follow-up and Halden Subset)

**This is the most useful document in the series. It directly answers the open question I flagged at the end of the meta-analysis review: whether the per-hour gain persists.** It largely does: a randomised design with record-based output and log-measured hours still shows a gain of about 8.5% at 24 months.

It also handles earlier critiques well:

- **Log data for unrecorded work.** It adds system log data to address the concern that timesheets understate the hours actually worked.
- **Registered mediation.** It registers the mediation analysis before the 24-month outcomes were available.
- **Conservative Halden reading.** It treats the Halden survivors as an upward-biased subset rather than an estimate for organisations in general.
- **Correct rebuttals.** Both rebuttals in Section 5 are substantially correct. The meta-analysis point confirms the concern I raised about the four long-follow-up studies.

There are four main problems:

1. Contamination in the control group, which the report observes but does not apply to its own estimates.
2. A mediation result described more strongly than the design allows.
3. A Summary that compares different measures.
4. Some data whose origin is unexplained.

## Arithmetic check

| Item | Calculation | Result | Paper |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per hour, timesheets (24 months) | 0.966 / 0.88 | 1.098 | +9.8% ✓ |
| Per hour, system logs (24 months) | 0.966 / 0.89 | 1.085 | +8.5% ✓ |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 | 100 | ✓ |
| Halden hours | 34.9 / 40.3 | 0.866 | −13.4% ✓ |
| Halden per hour | 0.968 / 0.866 | 1.118 | +11.8% ✓ |
| Decline in gain, like-for-like | (12.5 − 9.8) / 12.5 | 22% | "about a quarter" ≈ ✓ |
| Counter cost per contact | 12% more staff, output roughly at baseline | ≈ +12% | +9% ? |

The counter cost figure needs explaining. If 12% more staff at the same pay restores output to about its baseline, cost per contact should rise by about 12%, not 9%. The 9% would follow only if contacts handled rose *above* baseline, perhaps through recovered abandoned calls, or if the cost base includes non-staff costs. State the calculation.

## Major issues

### 1. The control offices' meeting audit contaminates the comparison

The report treats the month-15 meeting audit as a side observation. It is also a **contamination of the control arm**, and it affects the main estimate:

- Two of seven control offices adopted part of the treatment mechanism. By the report's own mediation result, that mechanism carries nearly half the effect.
- Their output per hour rose about 4.1%. Spread across seven control offices, that lifts the control mean by roughly 1.2 points in the affected period.
- That works against the treated–control difference. **Up to about 40% of the apparent decline from 12.5% to 9.8% could be control improvement, not fading of the treatment effect.** The exact share depends on how the 24-month estimate is constructed: a point estimate at month 24, or an average over a window.
- The offices are in the same county, so the audit may be learning from treated offices. That is precisely the contamination office-level randomisation was meant to prevent.

**Fixes:**

- Report a sensitivity analysis excluding the two audit offices.
- Revise the "consistent with some fading" sentence accordingly.
- Note that the two possible readings point in opposite directions. If the effect faded, novelty concerns gain weight. If the controls caught up, the gain is partly available without cutting hours.

**The meeting figures don't reconcile.** Control meeting time averages 7.2 h at baseline and 7.0 h at month 24. The two audit offices went from 7.1 h to 5.0 h. For the average to come out at 7.0, the other five control offices must have *risen*, from about 7.24 h to about 7.8 h. Alternatively, the audit offices' meetings crept back toward their old level by month 24. Either is important. The first is odd; the second bears on whether reorganisation sticks without the forcing device of shorter hours. Report the trajectory of meeting time in the audit offices.

### 2. The Summary compares different measures

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data." The 12.5% is a timesheet figure; the 8.5% is a log figure. The body handles this correctly: the like-for-like comparison is 12.5% to 9.8%. The Summary's version overstates the decline, 32% against 22%.

**Was log data available for earlier periods?** The system existed throughout the trial, so baseline and nine-month log hours might be recoverable.

- If so, report a log-based nine-month estimate.
- If not, explain how the log-based difference-in-differences gets its pre-period. Without baseline log hours, the −11% is not a difference-in-differences estimate.

**Overlapping confidence intervals.** The nine-month and 24-month intervals overlap heavily: +6.9% to +18.4% against +4.6% to +15.2%. The data cannot statistically distinguish the decline from no decline. "Consistent with some fading" is fair; anything stronger is not.

### 3. Log hours are a different measure, not just a stricter one

"Active log-in time on the case-management system" captures time spent working on cases. Several kinds of work happen off that system:

- meetings;
- phone calls;
- reading;
- training;
- paper-file work.

Log hours are therefore a subset of working time, not a fuller count of it.

**This affects the mediation result.** The outcome is output per log-measured hour. Meeting time is presumably *not* in that denominator. So cutting meetings does not mechanically raise output per log hour, as it would per timesheet hour. That actually makes the meetings result more interesting, because it implies a real effect on case-work efficiency, perhaps through less fragmentation of the working day. The report should say so, rather than leave readers to assume a mechanical link.

**"Slightly more work than timesheets" needs the same qualification.** Logs could show a smaller fall than timesheets because off-system work fell more, not because timesheets missed hours. Report baseline levels for both measures, not just the percentage changes.

### 4. The mediation result is described more strongly than the design allows

The Summary says the registered test "confirms" the meetings pathway. It supports the pathway; "confirms" overstates it.

- **Same offices, overlapping data.** The hypothesis came from these same seven treated offices. A registered test on the same units, with data that overlap the period that generated the hypothesis, is better than post hoc analysis but is not independent replication.
- **"A larger sample of office-months."** Office-months are not independent. The effective sample is still 14 offices. An interval of 28–66% looks narrow for 14 clusters. State how clustering was handled in the mediation model, for example a cluster bootstrap.
- **Uneven measurement error favours meetings.** Meeting time comes from calendars and is measured precisely. Fatigue comes from a self-report scale and carries more error. Measurement error attenuates a mediator's estimated share, so the fatigue share is likely understated relative to meetings. The finding that meetings matter "more than twice as much" is partly a measurement artifact.
- **Unmeasured co-occurring changes.** Halden managers also reported simplified approvals and the end of low-value reporting. Changes like these probably moved together with meeting cuts, so the meetings pathway may be absorbing them.
- **Staff turnover is a candidate for the unexplained 35%.** Annual resignations were about 4% in treated offices against about 8% in controls over two years. Treated offices therefore have more experienced staff on average, which could raise output independently of hours. Report the composition of staff by tenure, or adjust for it.

The tone of the meetings section ("since dismissed as post hoc") also reads as a reply to Varga & Holm. A neutral framing would serve the authors better, given they are testing their own earlier hypothesis.

### 5. Where did the baseline meeting and fatigue data come from?

The nine-month report had calendar data only for month six. It had no pre-period meeting data and no fatigue measure. This report gives:

- meeting time "from 7.4 to 3.9 between baseline and month 24";
- fatigue improving 0.34 SD "relative to control."

Explain both:

- **Meetings.** Were historical calendars recovered after the fact? If so, how complete is the recovery, and was it done before outcomes were known?
- **Fatigue.** When was the scale first given? If it was added at month 11 with the follow-up protocol, the 0.34 SD is a cross-sectional difference between arms, not a change. Mediation then rests on a mediator with no baseline.

## Halden subset

- **A further selection layer.** Fourteen of 23 organisations agreed to take part. Who declined, and were they the weaker performers? This adds selection on top of the two layers the report already names (completing the pilot, then choosing to continue).
- **Hours baseline.** The 40.3 h baseline matches the 27-organisation time-tracking group in Varga & Holm. Do all 11 continuing organisations have time tracking? If not, which hours figure is used?
- **"Upper bound" is stronger than the design supports.** Without a comparison group, secular trends could push either way. "Likely upward-biased" is defensible; a strict bound is not.
- **The Summary mislabels one reversion.** It says all three reverters had "client-facing or coverage obligations." The marketing agency cited client deadlines, which is discretionary work under the meta-analysis definition. It is a failure in discretionary work and should be reported as one, not folded into the coverage-bound story.
- **An intention-to-treat figure would help.** Including the three reverters at their output at reversion (88–91) gives a less flattering but more honest estimate for the 14 organisations.

## Smaller points

- **Counter arm.** Ending the arm at month 12 because of waiting times is itself a strong result. The months 10–12 comparison (7.3 against 4.0 minutes, treated against control) is properly controlled, which fixes a gap in the nine-month report.
- **The meeting audit as evidence.** The finding that 4.1% per 2.1 hours is comparable to the mediation-implied effect is interesting. But it is a before–after comparison in two offices, open to regression to the mean and seasonality. The report's caution is appropriate.
- **Independence.** Okafor (Halden) is a co-author, and the Varden authors are testing their own earlier hypothesis. A brief statement on independence would help, since the report adjudicates claims made against both groups.
- **Sick days.** Sick days fell 27% at 24 months. The question of how sick days are counted under the reduced schedule (fewer scheduled days mechanically means fewer recordable sick days) still hasn't been answered across the series.

## Suggested revisions

1. Add a sensitivity analysis excluding the two audit offices, and reinterpret the decline from 12.5% to 9.8% in that light.
2. Make the Summary like-for-like (12.5% to 9.8% on timesheets), and say whether nine-month log data exist.
3. Describe log hours accurately as on-system work time, and explain what that means for the mediation result.
4. Replace "confirms" with "supports." State how clustering and measurement error were handled, and consider staff tenure as a mediator.
5. Explain the origin of the baseline meeting and fatigue data.
6. Reconcile the control meeting-time averages with the audit offices' figures.
7. Show the counter cost-per-contact calculation.
8. Report an intention-to-treat figure for the Halden subset, and relabel the marketing agency reversion.

## Where the series now stands

| Question | Current best answer |
|---|---|
| Is there a per-hour gain in discretionary work? | Yes. About 8–10% on strict measures (randomised, record-based output, log hours, 24 months). |
| Does it persist? | Mostly, to 24 months. Some decline, possibly partly from control contamination. |
| Per-worker output? | Slightly below control (about −3%). The hours cut is mostly, not fully, offset. |
| Coverage-bound work? | Service worsens. The county ended the arm. |
| Mechanism? | Meeting reduction is the leading candidate, from a registered but non-independent test. Its share may be overstated relative to fatigue. |
| Can reorganisation alone capture the gain? | Untested. This needs a three-arm trial: hours cut, reorganisation only, and control. |

The last row is the natural next study. The meeting audit suggests it matters, and the report rightly says this trial cannot answer it.

I can sketch a design for that three-arm trial, or draft revised Summary and mediation sections, if that would help.
